title: Presale Search Cap
story: When concert presale opens, fans hammer the seat search, and some scripts refresh it hundreds of times a minute. The ticket site limits each fan to a few searches per clock minute. The counter for the 10:04 minute starts at zero at 10:04:00 and is discarded at 10:05:00, and a fan who goes over the limit receives HTTP 429 "Too Many Requests".

This is the fixed-window counter from Rate Limiting. It keeps one small counter per user per window, which is cheap enough to hold for millions of users in a shared in-memory store. Its known weakness is at the window edge, as the second example shows.
task: • constructor(limit, windowSec) sets the rule that each fan may make at most limit allowed requests per window.
• allow(fan, t) handles a request from fan at time t, in whole seconds. It returns true if the request is allowed and false if it is rejected.

Windows are fixed and aligned to 0: a request at time t falls in window number floor(t / windowSec), so with windowSec = 60 the windows are [0, 59], [60, 119], and so on. A request is allowed if the fan has had fewer than limit allowed requests in the same window. Rejected requests do not count. Each fan has separate counts.
constraints: 0 ≤ t ≤ 1,000,000,000, and t never decreases from one call to the next
fan is a non-empty string of up to 20 letters and digits

examples.explanation: Times 10, 20, 30 and 59 are in window 0 (0 to 59). The first three use up the limit of 3, so 59 is rejected. Time 60 starts window 1 with a fresh count.

Ben makes 2 requests at 58 and 59 in window 0, then 2 more at 60 and 61 in window 1. That is 4 requests in 4 seconds even though the limit is 2 per minute, and this burst at the window edge is the cost of fixed windows. Cy has her own count, so her request at 59 is allowed.

hints: For one fan, which earlier requests can affect whether the request at time t is allowed? Do requests from an earlier window matter?
Only the current window matters, so each fan needs two numbers: the window being counted and the number of allowed requests in it.
Keep a hash map from fan to [window, count]. When a request arrives in a different window than the stored one, reset the count to 0 for the new window.
Compute w = floor(t / windowSec). If the fan's stored window is not w, store [w, 0]. Then if the count is below the limit, add 1 and return true; otherwise return false without counting.
bruteForce: The brute force stores every allowed request time for each fan and counts the stored times in the same window on each request. With 2,000 calls that is up to 4 million checks, and the stored history grows without bound.
Only the current window matters, so keeping a single counter per fan makes both the time and the memory per fan constant.

walkthrough: Keep one counter per fan, tagged with the window it belongs to. A request that falls in a new window resets the counter.
Trace the first example, with limit 3 and window 60:
• At t = 10 the request is in window 0. Ana has nothing stored, so start [0, 0]. Since 0 < 3, the count becomes 1 and the request is allowed.
• At t = 20 and t = 30 the requests are still in window 0. The counts become 2 and 3, and both are allowed.
• At t = 59 the request is in window 0 and the count of 3 is not below 3, so it is rejected and the count stays 3.
• At t = 60 the request is in window 1, which differs from the stored 0, so the record resets to [1, 0]. The count becomes 1 and the request is allowed.
The weakness is that two windows meet at t = 60, so a fan can fit two full windows of requests into a few seconds. If that burst matters, use a sliding window, as in Password Reset Throttle.
solution.timeWhy: Each call does one map lookup and a few comparisons.
solution.spaceWhy: One small record is stored for each of the f fans seen. A real system lets each record expire at the end of its window.
solution.takeaway: A fixed-window limiter keeps one counter per key per window. It is small and fast, but it can allow up to twice the limit across a window edge. Store the window number next to the count so that a new window resets it.
